members.summary: Configuration for the Terminal Velocity Matching family.

parameters.name: sample_size
parameters.description:
Side of the latent the network operates on — `32` for
256-pixel ImageNet, `64` for 512-pixel, after the Stable
Diffusion VAE's factor of eight.

parameters.name: in_channels
parameters.description:
Latent channels.  The network predicts a velocity in the latent's
own space, which the loss and the sampler add to the input, so
the two must be equal.

parameters.name: out_channels
parameters.description:
Latent channels.  The network predicts a velocity in the latent's
own space, which the loss and the sampler add to the input, so
the two must be equal.

parameters.name: patch_size
parameters.description: Side of the square patch each token covers.

parameters.name: hidden_size
parameters.description: Transformer width.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: Number of transformer blocks.

parameters.name: num_heads
parameters.description:
Attention heads per block.  DiT-XL uses 16; the paper uses 18 so
the head dimension is 64, which its attention kernel runs 1.25x
faster at, and reports the two train to the same FID.

parameters.name: mlp_ratio
parameters.description: Feed-forward expansion inside each block.

parameters.name: frequency_embedding_size
parameters.description:
Width of the sinusoid each scalar condition is expanded into
before its MLP.

parameters.name: num_classes
parameters.description:
Label vocabulary.  Index `num_classes` is the null label the
guidance dropout substitutes.

parameters.name: class_dropout
parameters.description:
Probability of training a sample unconditionally — its label is
replaced by the null token and its guidance scale by one.

parameters.name: qk_norm
parameters.description:
RMS-normalise queries and keys (with a learnable scale) before
attention.  Part of the semi-Lipschitz control.

parameters.name: modulation_norm
parameters.description:
RMS-normalise each adaLN shift, scale and gate vector (Eq. 16 and
Appendix B.2).  Without it the modulation's magnitude, and with it
the layer's Lipschitz constant, can grow unbounded — the
activation blow-up of Figure 4.

parameters.name: time_embedding_init
parameters.description:
How the time and guidance MLPs start.  Every other linear layer
is initialised to unit spectral norm regardless.

parameters.name: guidance_scale
parameters.description:
The classifier-free guidance weight $w$ trained at, and the
default a sampler uses for labelled draws.  The paper's best
one-step 256-pixel model trains at `2.0`.

parameters.name: guidance_range
parameters.description:
`(w_min, w_max)` to train with a random guidance weight instead
of a constant one: $\beta = 1/w$ is drawn uniformly from
$[1/w_{\max}, 1/w_{\min}]$.  Constant guidance wins in every
comparison the paper makes (Table 4a), which is why `None`.

parameters.name: scaled_parameterization
parameters.description:
Predict $F$ with the guidance weight factored out, so the
model's velocity is $w\,F_\theta$ (Table 4c).

parameters.name: time_sampler
parameters.description: Joint distribution of `(t, s)`.

parameters.name: gap_mean
parameters.description: Logit-normal parameters of `t - s` under `"gap"`.

parameters.name: gap_std
parameters.description: Logit-normal parameters of `t - s` under `"gap"`.

parameters.name: t_mean
parameters.description:
Logit-normal parameters of `t` under `"trunc"` and `"clamp"`
— Table 3's best setting for both.

parameters.name: t_std
parameters.description:
Logit-normal parameters of `t` under `"trunc"` and `"clamp"`
— Table 3's best setting for both.

parameters.name: s_mean
parameters.description:
Logit-normal parameters of `s`, and of the Flow Matching time
when that is drawn separately.

parameters.name: s_std
parameters.description:
Logit-normal parameters of `s`, and of the Flow Matching time
when that is drawn separately.

parameters.name: separate_flow_matching_time
parameters.description:
Draw the Flow Matching term's time independently of the pair
instead of reusing `s` — the sampler the paper names `gap*`,
which lets the Flow Matching term keep the time distribution that
works for Flow Matching on its own (Figure 9).

parameters.name: ratio_t_equals_s
parameters.description:
Fraction of the batch trained with `s = t`, where the terminal
term vanishes and only Flow Matching remains.  The paper finds any
non-zero share hurts one-step quality (Table 4d).

parameters.name: target_ema_decay
parameters.description:
$\gamma$, the EMA rate of the network that supplies the
terminal and unconditional targets.  `0` uses the live weights
under a stop-gradient; `0.99` is the paper's sweet spot
(Table 4b).

parameters.name: eval_ema_decay
parameters.description:
$\gamma^{**}$, the rate of Algorithm 1's second average, the
one that is evaluated and released (Table 6, "Eval EMA rate").
`None` keeps no such copy, saving a network's worth of memory.

parameters.name: detach_jvp
parameters.description:
Stop the gradient at $\partial_s F_\theta$.  Faster and
lighter, but biases the gradient — the paper's runtime study
offers it as a trade, not a default (Figure 10).

parameters.name: latent_mean
parameters.description:
Per-channel statistics the VAE latent is whitened with before the
network sees it, $z = (\ell - \mu)/\sigma$ — IMM's setting,
which the paper follows (Appendix F.1), in place of the usual
single factor 0.18215.  The defaults are the 256-pixel ones; the
512-pixel latent has its own.

parameters.name: latent_std
parameters.description:
Per-channel statistics the VAE latent is whitened with before the
network sees it, $z = (\ell - \mu)/\sigma$ — IMM's setting,
which the paper follows (Appendix F.1), in place of the usual
single factor 0.18215.  The defaults are the 256-pixel ones; the
512-pixel latent has its own.

examples:
>>> from lucid.models.generative.tvm import TVMConfig
>>> config = TVMConfig()
>>> config.hidden_size, config.depth, config.num_heads
(1152, 28, 18)
>>> config.num_patches
256
The 512-pixel model is the same network over a wider latent:
>>> TVMConfig(sample_size=64).num_patches
1024
notes:
Reference: Zhou, Parger, Haque, and Song, *"Terminal Velocity
Matching"*, ICLR 2026 ([arXiv:2511.19797](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19797)).  Training settings are
Table 6; the defaults here are its first column, the 256-pixel model
at $w = 2$ behind the 3.29 one-step FID.

The released code agrees with the paper on every setting above, with
one exception it does not exercise: its random-guidance path draws
$w$ rather than $1/w$ uniformly.  The paper's
description is followed here.

methods.name: __init__
methods.summary: Initialise the model. See the class docstring for parameters.

methods.name: target_network
methods.summary: The EMA network $\theta^*$ the targets are read from.
methods.extended:
With `TVMConfig.target_ema_decay` at zero this is the live
network itself, used under a stop-gradient — Table 4b's
$\gamma = 0$.

methods.name: ema_network
methods.summary: The evaluation EMA $\theta^{**}$ — what Algorithm 1 outputs.

raises.description:
If `TVMConfig.eval_ema_decay` is `None`, so no
evaluation average is kept.

methods.name: update_ema
methods.summary: Advance both of Algorithm 1's averages by one step.
methods.extended:
$\theta^* \leftarrow \gamma^*\theta^* + (1 - \gamma^*)\theta$
and $\theta^{**} \leftarrow \gamma^{**}\theta^{**} + (1 - \gamma^{**})\theta$, over parameters only — the released
training loop averages nothing else, and this network has no
persistent buffers.  Call it after each optimiser step.

The averages are evaluated once they are written.  They are
outside `parameters`, so neither the optimiser's flush nor a
loop's reaches them on Metal.

methods.name: forward
methods.signature: forward(images: Tensor, labels: Tensor | None = None)
methods.summary: One training step of the TVM objective (Eq. 15).

parameters.name: images
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` — the data, here the VAE latent of it.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description:
`(B,)` class indices.  Each is replaced by the null label
with probability `TVMConfig.class_dropout`, and that
sample trains at $w = 1$.  `None` trains the
unconditional field throughout.

returns.description: The loss and its two terms.

notes:
Per sample, with $\beta = 1/w$,



$$
\beta^2\Bigl\lVert \tfrac{d}{ds} f_\theta(x_t, t, s)
  - u_{\theta^*}\bigl(\mathrm{sg}[x_t + f_\theta(x_t, t, s)],
  s\bigr)\Bigr\rVert^2 \mathbb{1}_{t \ne s}
+ \beta^2\bigl\lVert u_\theta(x_{s'}, s')
  - \bigl[w\,v + (1 - w)\,u_{\theta^*}(x_{s'}, s', \varnothing,
  1)\bigr]\bigr\rVert^2 .
$$

Squared norms are averaged over elements, as the released
training code computes them; the paper's sum differs by the
constant $CHW$.

methods.name: generate
methods.signature: generate(n_samples: int = 1, labels: Tensor | None = None, steps: int = 1, guidance_scale: float | None = None, noise: Tensor | None = None, device: str | None = None, use_ema: bool = False)
methods.summary: Jump from noise to data in `steps` evaluations.

parameters.name: n_samples
parameters.description: How many to draw.

parameters.name: labels
parameters.description:
`(n_samples,)` class indices.  `None` samples the
unconditional field.

parameters.name: steps
parameters.description:
Network evaluations.  $[0, 1]$ is split evenly and each
piece is one jump $x_s = x_t + (s - t)\,w F_\theta(x_t, t, s)$; the same network serves every step count, from one up
to the ODE limit, without retraining.

parameters.name: guidance_scale
parameters.description:
$w$.  `None` uses the weight the model was trained at
for labelled draws and one for unlabelled ones.

parameters.name: noise
parameters.description: Starting point $x_1$.  Drawn when absent.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Where to draw.  Defaults to the model's own device.

parameters.name: use_ema
parameters.description:
Sample from the evaluation EMA $\theta^{**}$ rather than
the live weights — what the paper evaluates after training.  A
loaded checkpoint already *is* that average, so the default
samples from the live network.

returns.description:
`samples` of shape `(n_samples, out_channels, H, W)` — a
latent, for the Stable Diffusion VAE to decode.

examples:
>>> from lucid.models import tvm_imagenet256_gen
>>> model = tvm_imagenet256_gen(sample_size=8, hidden_size=32, depth=2, num_heads=4)
>>> model.eval().generate(2, steps=4).samples.shape
(2, 4, 8, 8)

methods.name: from_vae_latent
methods.summary: Whiten a Stable Diffusion VAE latent the way the model was trained.

parameters.name: latent
parameters.description:
`(B, C, H, W)` — a sample from the VAE posterior,
$\ell = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x)\,\epsilon$, which is
what the released pipeline encodes images into (not the
posterior mean).

returns.description:
$z = (\ell - \mu) / \sigma$ per channel — the `images`
`forward` trains on.  `to_vae_latent` inverts it.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models import tvm_imagenet256_gen
>>> model = tvm_imagenet256_gen(sample_size=8, hidden_size=32, depth=2, num_heads=4)
>>> model.from_vae_latent(lucid.zeros((1, 4, 8, 8))).shape
(1, 4, 8, 8)

methods.name: to_vae_latent
methods.summary: Undo the per-channel whitening the model's latents carry.

parameters.name: samples
parameters.description: `(B, C, H, W)` — `generate`'s output.

returns.description:
$\ell = z\,\sigma + \mu$ with the statistics in
`TVMConfig.latent_mean` / `TVMConfig.latent_std` —
the raw latent the Stable Diffusion VAE's decoder expects.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models import tvm_imagenet256_gen
>>> model = tvm_imagenet256_gen(sample_size=8, hidden_size=32, depth=2, num_heads=4)
>>> model.to_vae_latent(lucid.zeros((1, 4, 8, 8))).shape
(1, 4, 8, 8)
notes:
The released models were trained on `stabilityai/sd-vae-ft-ema`
posterior samples whitened per channel, not scaled by 0.18215, so
decoding a sample without this step yields saturated noise.
`lucid.models.generative.stable_diffusion.AutoencoderKL`
is that decoder.

members.summary: TVM's objective and its one- and few-step sampler.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: The variant to build.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.tvm import (
...     TVMConfig, TVMForImageGeneration)
>>> config = TVMConfig(sample_size=8, patch_size=2, hidden_size=32,
...                    depth=2, num_heads=4, num_classes=10)
>>> model = TVMForImageGeneration(config).eval()
>>> model.generate(2, labels=lucid.tensor([1, 2])).samples.shape
(2, 4, 8, 8)
notes:
Reference: Zhou, Parger, Haque, and Song, *"Terminal Velocity
Matching"*, ICLR 2026 ([arXiv:2511.19797](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19797)).  Training is Algorithm 1
with the objective of Eq. 15; sampling is Figure 3.

**Call** `update_ema` **once per optimiser step.**  Algorithm 1
keeps two exponential moving averages of the weights and updates both
after every step: $\theta^*$ at
`TVMConfig.target_ema_decay`, which the terminal target and the
unconditional half of the guided velocity are read off, and
$\theta^{**}$ at `TVMConfig.eval_ema_decay`, the model
that is evaluated and that the released checkpoints are.  Only the
caller knows when an optimiser step has happened.

Both copies are created from the live weights the first time either
is needed — the first training step reads $\theta^*$, so that
is $\theta^* \leftarrow \theta,\ \theta^{**} \leftarrow \theta$ at initialisation, as Algorithm 1 has it — and both are kept
outside the module tree: not parameters, not in `state_dict`,
not counted.  They are training state, like an optimiser's moments;
`target_network` and `ema_network` expose them for
checkpointing.  Loading weights into the network — through
`load_state_dict` here or on `tvm` — restarts both from the
loaded weights, so to resume a run load the network first and the
averages' own checkpoints after it.

members.summary: The two-time velocity network $w\,F_\theta(x_t, t, s, c, w)$.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: The variant to build.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.generative.tvm import TVMConfig, TVMModel
>>> config = TVMConfig(sample_size=8, patch_size=2, hidden_size=32,
...                    depth=2, num_heads=4, num_classes=10)
>>> model = TVMModel(config).eval()
>>> x = lucid.randn((1, 4, 8, 8))
>>> t, s = lucid.tensor([1.0]), lucid.tensor([0.0])
>>> model(x, t, s, lucid.tensor([3])).sample.shape
(1, 4, 8, 8)
notes:
Reference: Zhou, Parger, Haque, and Song, *"Terminal Velocity
Matching"*, ICLR 2026 ([arXiv:2511.19797](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19797)), Sections 3–4 and
Appendix F.1.

The forward returns the **average velocity over** $[s, t]$ —
the displacement divided by its length — so that one step of the
sampler is $x_s = x_t + (s - t)\cdot\mathrm{sample}$.  Under the
scaled parameterisation that is $w\,F_\theta$, the network's
output times the guidance weight; otherwise it is $F_\theta$
itself.  At $s = t$ it is the instantaneous velocity
$u_\theta(x_t, t)$.

>>> from lucid.models.generative.tvm._model import TVMOutput

attributes.name: loss
attributes.description:
The objective of Eq. 15, a scalar — the two terms below, summed
per sample and averaged over the batch.

attributes.name: terminal_loss
attributes.description:
The batch mean of the terminal-velocity term, $\lVert \frac{d}{ds} f_\theta - u_{\theta^*}(\hat x_s, s)\rVert^2 / w^2$.
Zero for samples drawn with $s = t$.

attributes.name: flow_matching_loss
attributes.description:
The batch mean of the guided Flow Matching term.  Reported apart
because the two move differently: Flow Matching settles early
while the terminal term keeps falling, and a terminal term that
stalls while Flow Matching is fine is the first sign of a bad
target EMA.

summary: Terminal Velocity Matching — one- and few-step generation from scratch.
extended:
Zhou, Parger, Haque and Song, ICLR 2026 ([arXiv:2511.19797](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19797)).  MeanFlow's
dual: where MeanFlow differentiates the learned displacement at the
interval's start, TVM differentiates it at the terminal time and matches
it to the velocity where the jump lands — an objective that bounds the
2-Wasserstein distance once the network is made Lipschitz, which is what
its RMS-normalised DiT is for.
citation: Zhou, Linqi, Mathias Parger, Ayaan Haque, and Jiaming Song. "Terminal Velocity Matching." International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2026.  [arXiv:2511.19797](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19797).
theory:
Write the ground-truth flow map from time $t$ to time $s$
as $\psi(x_t, t, s) = x_t + \int_t^s u(x_r, r)\,dr$ and its net
displacement as $f(x_t, t, s) = \psi(x_t, t, s) - x_t$.  The
displacement satisfies two conditions: it *is* the integral, and its
derivative at $s = t$ is the instantaneous velocity.  One
two-time network parameterises both,



$$
f_\theta(x_t, t, s) = (s - t)\,F_\theta(x_t, t, s), \qquad
u_\theta(x_t, t) = F_\theta(x_t, t, t),
$$

and the scaling $(s - t)$ makes $f_\theta(x_t, t, t) = 0$
hold by construction.

The integral condition cannot be trained directly — it would need an
ODE solve per sample.  Differentiating it with respect to the
**terminal** time $s$ instead gives a condition with no
integral in it,



$$
\frac{d}{ds} f(x_t, t, s) = u\bigl(\psi(x_t, t, s), s\bigr),
$$

and the squared error in that condition, integrated over
$s \in [0, t]$, upper-bounds the displacement error.  The
unknowns on the right are replaced by the model itself — the jump
lands at $x_t + f_\theta(x_t, t, s)$ and the velocity there is
$u_\theta$ — which is only sound if $u_\theta$ is right,
so Flow Matching is trained jointly.  It is the same condition at
zero displacement:



$$
\mathcal{L}^{t,s}_{\mathrm{TVM}}
= \Bigl\lVert \tfrac{d}{ds} f_\theta(x_t, t, s)
  - u_{\theta^*}\!\bigl(x_t + f_{\theta}(x_t, t, s), s\bigr)
  \Bigr\rVert^2
+ \bigl\lVert u_\theta(x_s, s) - v_s \bigr\rVert^2 .
$$

$\theta^*$ is an exponential moving average of the weights,
held under a stop-gradient, and the derivative expands to
$F_\theta + (s - t)\,\partial_s F_\theta$ — one Jacobian-vector
product along $s$, whose result is itself back-propagated
through.  A weighted integral of this objective over $s$ bounds
$W_2^2$ between the data and the model's push-forward when
$u_\theta(\cdot, s)$ is Lipschitz (Theorem 1).

**MeanFlow's dual.**  MeanFlow enforces
$\frac{d}{dt} f_\theta = -u(x_t, t)$, differentiating at the
*start*; the tangent of that derivative contains the sampled velocity
$v_t$, whose magnitude under guidance varies widely.  TVM's
tangent is a unit step in $s$, independent of $x_t$ and
$t$, which is why it trains stably even with random guidance.

**Guidance is learned, not applied.**  The class-conditional field is
the guided one, $w\,u(x, r, c) + (1 - w)\,u(x, r)$, with the
unconditional half supplied by the EMA network.  Its magnitude grows
linearly in $w$, so the loss is weighted by $1/w^2$ and
the network optionally predicts $F$ with the factor $w$
pulled out — the *scaled parameterisation*.

**Semi-Lipschitz control.**  Every LayerNorm becomes a parameter-free
RMSNorm, queries and keys are RMS-normalised, every adaLN modulation
vector is itself RMS-normalised so its scale cannot grow without
bound, and linear layers start at unit spectral norm.

**Where Lucid departs from the authors' release, on purpose.**  The
model matches the authors' code to float32 rounding (forward pass,
terminal derivative, loss, every gradient and the sampler), but three
choices differ, and they matter to anyone reproducing a released run
from scratch:

* *The patch embedding starts at unit spectral norm.*  Lucid divides
  the patch-embedding weight by its largest singular value, as the
  paper prescribes for linear layers.  The release's initialiser
  divides a rebound alias of the weight (`w.data = w.data / s[0]`)
  rather than the parameter, so its patch embedding keeps the
  Xavier-normal draw, $\sigma_{\max} \approx 1.53$ at full size.
* *Precision.*  The release trains under bf16 autocast, and its
  Jacobian-vector product runs attention in bf16 even when autocast
  is off.  Lucid computes in the model's own dtype throughout —
  float32 unless the model is cast — including the terminal
  derivative.  A converted checkpoint sampled in Lucid is therefore
  not rounded where the authors' bf16 sampler is.
* *No NaN masking.*  The release replaces a NaN loss with zero before
  the backward pass; Lucid returns the loss as computed, so a
  diverging step is seen instead of trained through.
